title: Equivariant rationalization of the generic curve marking
statement:
Let $k$ be a field, $S$ a normal integral projective finite-type $k$-scheme, $K=k(S)$, and $f:X\to S$ an H-projective morphism with $X$ integral of finite type over $k$. Assume all geometric fibres of $f$ are pure of dimension one and $C=X_K$ is smooth and geometrically integral. Put $F=k(X)$. Assume $X$ is normal. Let $M\subset C$ be a reduced finite etale closed subscheme, and let a finite group $G$ act compatibly on $k,X,S,f$, preserving $M$; nonfaithful semilinear actions are allowed. There is a finite extension $K'/K$, Galois over $B=K^G$, containing $K$ and images of all the finitely many residue fields of $M$. Set
$$G'=\{(g,\sigma)\in G\times\operatorname{Aut}_B(K'):\sigma|_K=g|_K\},\qquad N=\ker(G'\to G).$$
The projection $G'\to G$ is surjective, $N=\operatorname{Aut}_K(K')$, and $(K')^N=K$. The tensor product $F'=F\otimes_KK'$ is a field finite separable over $F$. Put $S'=\operatorname{Nor}_{K'}(S)$ and $X'=\operatorname{Nor}_{F'}(X)$. Then $S'$ is normal integral projective of finite type over $k$, $X'$ is normal integral of finite type over $k$, and $S'\to S$ and $X'\to X\times_SS'$ are finite surjective. The morphism $X'\to S'$ is H-projective with pure one-dimensional geometric fibres and generic fibre $C\times_KK'$, smooth and geometrically integral. The action
$$(g,\sigma)(z\otimes c)=g(z)\otimes\sigma(c)$$
extends compatibly to these models, and $(F')^N=F$. The reduced inverse image of $M$ on the generic fibre is a finite set of distinct $K'$-rational points stable under $G'$. The construction allows $M=\varnothing$. For every integer $b\geq0$, if the normalizations of all reduced irreducible components of all geometric fibres of $X/S$ have genus at least $b$, then the same holds for $X'/S'$. More precisely, for a geometric point $s':\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to S'$ and its image $s$ in $S$, every reduced irreducible component $Z'$ of $X'_{s'}$ maps finitely and nonconstantly onto a reduced irreducible component $Z$ of $X_s$, and the induced map of smooth proper normalizations is nonconstant with $g((Z')^\nu)\geq g(Z^\nu)$. Here both fibres are taken over the same algebraically closed field $\Omega$.

Normal means that every local ring is an integrally closed domain. H-projective means admitting a closed immersion into a finite-dimensional projective space over the target. A finite separable field extension is finite-dimensional with separable minimal polynomials. A finite Galois extension is a finite normal separable extension; normal for fields means that every irreducible polynomial over the smaller field with a root in the larger field splits there. For a group $G$ acting on a field $V$, $V^G$ is the subfield of elements fixed by every member of $G$. All fixed-field equalities below use the field embeddings induced by the displayed scheme maps. The notions used are [def-weil-field], [def-pc-integral-scheme], [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], [def-kun-projective], [def-sc-function-field], [def-pc-field-extension], [def-weil-pure-dimension], [def-weil-geometric-fibre], [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], [def-pc-geometrically-irreducible], [def-fin-normalization-extension], [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism], [def-weil-surjective-morphism], [def-pc-fibre-product], [def-weil-etale-morphism], [def-pc-genus].

proof.text: Apply the etale-fibre description to $M\to\operatorname{Spec}K$, taking the fibre at the unique point. Since $M$ is finite, the resulting discrete decomposition is finite: $M=\coprod_{j=1}^r\operatorname{Spec}L_j$, where each $L_j/K$ is finite separable. Choose a primitive element $a_j$ of each $L_j/K$, with monic separable minimal polynomial $p_j$. Thus $K[T]/(p_j)\simeq L_j$. If $M$ is empty take $r=0$, with no polynomials.

proof.text: Apply the equivariant polynomial-envelope theorem with $H=G$, its given (possibly nonfaithful) action on $K$, $I=\{1,\ldots,r\}$, $f_j=p_j$, and one field factor $L_j$ for each $j$. Its hypotheses are exactly the presentations from Step 1, and its fixed field is $B=K^G$. It gives $K\subseteq K\prime$ finite Galois over both $K$ and $B$, embeddings of all $L_j$, complete linear factorizations of the $p_j$, and exactly the displayed finite group $G\prime$. Its surjectivity and kernel assertions give $G\prime\twoheadrightarrow G$, $N=\operatorname{Aut}_K(K\prime)$ and $(K\prime)^N=K$. Its empty-index case applies when $r=0$.

source.place: Tags 09I3 (lemma-galois-over-fixed-field), 0BME (lemma-lift-maps); finite equivariant splitting through the cited polynomial-envelope statement.

proof.text: Apply the constant-extension case of the finite normal relative curve-model theorem, with $E=K\prime$ and $L=F\otimes_KK\prime$. Its hypotheses on $S,X,f$ and the smooth geometrically integral generic curve are precisely those in the statement here. It says this tensor product is a field finite separable over $F$, and its constant-extension clause identifies the normalized generic curve with $C\times_KK\prime$. It supplies all stated normality, integrality, finite-type, projectivity, finite-surjectivity and pure-geometric-fibre assertions for $S\prime=\operatorname{Nor}_{K\prime}(S)$ and $X\prime=\operatorname{Nor}_{F\prime}(X)$. In particular the generic curve is smooth and geometrically integral.

source.place: Tags 0307 (lemma-integral-closure-localize), 034L (lemma-integral-closure-in-normal); the cited relative normal-model theorem includes the constant-extension field and pure-fibre assertions.

proof.text: The displayed action is well defined on the tensor product: $g(za)\otimes\sigma(c)=g(z)g(a)\otimes\sigma(c)=g(z)\otimes\sigma(ac)$ for $a\in K$, since $\sigma|_K=g|_K$. Multiplication, identity and composition are checked on pure tensors, and inverse pairs give inverses. It agrees with the given actions on $F$ and $K\prime$; hence the semilinear functoriality clause of the relative normal-model theorem extends it compatibly to $X\prime,S\prime$. For $(1,\sigma)\in N$ it is $\mathrm{id}_F\otimes\sigma$. The tensor-invariants theorem applied to the $K$-vector space $F$ and the fixed-field equality from Step 2 gives $(F\prime)^N=F\otimes1$, identified with $F$.

source.place: Tag 038B (lemma-closed-fixed-by-Galois), tensor invariants; normalization functoriality in the cited normal-model theorem.

proof.text: For each $j$, the $K\prime$-algebra $L_j\otimes_KK\prime$ has the presentation $K\prime[T]/(p_j)$: both algebras represent an element satisfying $p_j=0$, so the maps sending the generator to $a_j\otimes1$ and back are inverse. The split roots from Step 2 are distinct, since $p_j$ is separable (its Bezout identity with its derivative stays valid over $K\prime$). Apply the distinct-linear-factor quotient theorem to obtain $L_j\otimes_KK\prime\simeq\prod_{\deg p_j}K\prime$. Taking spectra of these presentations gives the inverse image of $M$ as a disjoint union of distinct $K\prime$-points, already reduced. It is $G\prime$-stable: the generic-fibre map is equivariant and $M$ is $G$-stable, so every action sends its inverse image to itself. The empty coproduct remains empty.

proof.text: Fix $s\prime:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to S\prime$ and let $s$ be its composite to $S$. Base change the finite map $X\prime\to X\times_SS\prime$ to get a finite $\Omega$-map $h:X\prime_{s\prime}\to X_s$. For a reduced irreducible component $Z\prime$ of its source, the restricted map to $X_s$ is finite: on affine charts quotienting a finite algebra by the component prime is still finite. The image is closed, since finite maps are proper and proper maps have closed image; write its reduced integral image as $Z$. On an affine meeting the image this gives an injective finite map of domains $A/\ker(A\to D)\hookrightarrow D$. The nonempty-open dimension theorem identifies affine-chart dimensions with the dimensions of these integral finite-type curves; equality of dimension for injective integral extensions therefore gives $\dim Z=\dim Z\prime=1$. Since $X_s$ is pure one-dimensional, an irreducible closed subset of dimension one is a component. Thus $Z\prime\to Z$ is finite surjective and nonconstant. These are fibres over the same $\Omega$, by the fibre-product identification.

The curves $Z\prime,Z$ are projective: they are reduced closed subschemes of the projective fibres of $f\prime,f$, respectively, so compose their closed immersions with the chosen projective embeddings. Projectivity of those fibres follows from projective base change; projective implies proper. The normalization-properties theorem makes $(Z\prime)^
u,Z^
u$ proper smooth integral curves, because $\Omega$ is algebraically closed and hence perfect; their dimensions are one. Both normalizations are integral and of finite type over $\Omega$, since $
u$ is finite. The source $(Z\prime)^
u$ has integrally closed local rings: over an affine open $\operatorname{Spec}D$ of $Z\prime$ it is $\operatorname{Spec}\overline D$, with $\overline D$ the integral closure of $D$ in $\operatorname{Frac}D=\operatorname{Frac}\overline D$, and a localization of an integrally closed domain is integrally closed. Apply dominant lifting through normalization to the dominant composite $(Z\prime)^
u	o Z\prime	o Z$ of two surjections to obtain the unique induced dominant, hence nonconstant map $(Z\prime)^
u	o Z^
u$. For each normalization, $\Omega$ is algebraically closed in its function field (an algebraic element over an algebraically closed field already lies in that field). The field geometric-irreducibility theorem and its generic-point criterion therefore give geometric irreducibility. The perfect-field reducedness theorem gives geometric reducedness. Hence both are geometrically integral, as required by genus monotonicity. The genus-monotonicity theorem gives $g((Z\prime)^
u)\ge g(Z^
u)$, including inseparable maps. Consequently every lower bound $b\ge0$ on the latter genera is inherited by $X\prime/S\prime$.
